profiles.name: Personal & Professional Development
profiles.actualContent: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
profiles.judgment: First-year personal, academic and professional development; genuine required UCR component without added natural-science credit claims.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: Required PPD

profiles.name: Research Methods & Statistics
profiles.actualContent: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
profiles.judgment: Research design, statistics and group research. Useful general methods; not chemical instrumentation or an individual physical-chemistry research project.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: provides research design, experimental logic and descriptive and inferential statistics

profiles.name: Introduction to Data Science
profiles.actualContent: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
profiles.judgment: Data wrangling, analysis and visualisation; genuine computational support, not chemical analysis laboratory practice.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops data cleaning, visualisation and analysis across varied scientific datasets

profiles.name: Machine Learning
profiles.actualContent: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.
profiles.judgment: Regression, classification, resampling and tree-based machine learning; possible scientific applications do not establish the underlying physics or chemistry.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops regression, resampling and predictive methods applicable to molecular and biomedical data

profiles.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
profiles.actualContent: Image Processing and Computer Vision deals with extracting high-level structural understanding from digital image and video data. As such, it aims to automate the task of the human visual system. In the broadest sense, Image Processing and Computer Vision studies methods for acquiring, processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. The course starts with a concise introduction into cameras, color models, and various image models and representations, but focuses on the processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. Image processing and analysis have many applications, inside as well as outside of robotics. An important application domain is medical imaging, where the goal is to reveal internal structures to diagnose and treat disease. Another application is remote sensing which aims to detect objects on earth. Image processing and analysis study methods that turn images into better images and aim to identify simple features in images. The course considers histograms, point operators, and local, edge, and morphological filters. It covers the Hough transform for detection of lines and curves, detection of corners, shapes and regions, and segmentation. Image understanding concerns the recognition of objects in images. The course introduces feature detection and tracking and object localization, classification, and evaluation. The Image Processing and Computer Vision course offers ample time to practice with the image processing, image analysis, and image understanding methods that are presented.
profiles.judgment: Computer vision and image processing, including medical applications. Not physical microscopy, spectroscopy or their instrument theory.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops image-processing and computer-vision methods relevant to biological and biomedical imaging

profiles.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
profiles.actualContent: Neural networks have enabled major advances in areas such as computer vision, large language models, and generative AI. This course focuses on the underlying theory as well as practical implementations in the Python programming language using packages such as TensorFlow . No familiarity with Python is assumed, but a willingness to learn and write code in Python is essential. In the first part of the course, w e start by building and training our own basic neural networks from scratch. We also use TensorFlow to create bigger networks and apply them to tabular data. In the second part of the course, we move on to more complex neural networks for applications such as computer vision and text classification . We also discuss recent developments in large language models (such as ChatGPT) . Finally, if time per mits, we have a brief look at image generation models (such as DALL-E).
profiles.judgment: Neural networks, TensorFlow and computational learning; not biophysical neurons, neurophysics or quantum theory.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops neural-network methods and practical Python implementation for complex scientific data

profiles.name: Introduction to Programming
profiles.actualContent: This is the gateway course of Computer Science and AI studies; an introductory course in problem solving and computer programming in Python. The course begins by introducing traditional structured programming and data constructs (i.e. branching, loops, functions; tuples and lists). Then consideration is given to testing and debugging and finally the object- oriented programming constructs. During the entire semester, elements of discrete mathematics (e.g., logic, sets, enumeration) as well as certain computational problem solving techniques are also incorporated into the course material. There are classes twice a week. The first half of each class is a lecture where we learn new material, while the second half is devoted to laboratory work where students tackle programming exercises and demonstrate their work. Homework comprises weekly programming exercises and online quizzes. Two larger programming projects are undertaken. There is a written Midterm exam and a written Final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with the Python programming language as well as important concepts of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving techniques.
profiles.judgment: Python programming is a genuine quantitative foundation; distinct from molecular or physical experimental methods.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: builds Python programming and computational problem-solving for scientific data

profiles.name: Mathematical Methods
profiles.actualContent: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3
profiles.judgment: Calculus, complex numbers and differential equations support science. Applications to physics do not constitute a physics sequence.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: provides calculus, linear algebra and differential-equation methods used across natural science

profiles.name: Linear Algebra
profiles.actualContent: Linear algebra is the study of systems of linear equations and linear functions. Systematic methods exist to solve such systems of linear equations. Matrices and vectors are introduced as the equivalent of a system of linear equations. This equivalence allows for reducing problems involving linear combinations of vectors to questions about systems of linear equations. The spanning of a (sub)space, linear independence and linear transformations are fundamental concepts in linear algebra. Matrix operations and theorems involving matrices will provide the basic tools for handling many applications of linear algebra. The invertible matrix theorem is a theorem of particular importance. The determinant of a matrix is an important scalar quantity related to the invertibility criterion for square matrices. Furthermore, the determinant is a measure for the amount by which a linear transformation changes the area of a ﬁgure. In multi-variable calculus, this measure is deﬁned as the Jacobian of a transformation. Introducing the more abstract concept of vector spaces allows for further generalization of these ideas. Many vector spaces resemble the well-known vector space Rn. In this course, the theory of vector spaces will be applied to the processing of discrete signals (Fourier Series), diﬀerence equations and Markov chains. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are used to understand the action of a linear transformation. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors arise naturally in diﬀerent areas of physics and mathematics.
profiles.judgment: Linear algebra, matrices, vector spaces, eigenvectors and transforms: genuine mathematical support, not quantum mechanics or electromagnetism.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops matrices, vectors and linear systems used in scientific modelling and data analysis

profiles.name: Computational & Numerical Methods
profiles.actualContent: Many problems in science and engineering presented in a mathematical format do not have exact analyt- ical solutions; these problems can only be solved numerically. The nature of the mathematical problem dictates the type of numerical algorithm to use; solving an optimization problem requires a different al- gorithm than solving a differential equation. The prerequisite gateway courseMathematical Methods introduces techniques and methods for solving equations in one variable, for finding derivatives of func- tions, or for solving integrals,etc., analytically. This course focuses on the same mathematical concepts but from a numerical and computational perspective. Numerical solutions obtained through some al- gorithm pose the following challenge: what does the output mean? How sensitive is the algorithm to a wrong input? There are examples showing that numerical algorithms can produce completely wrong and unexpected outputs resulting in a disaster. Numerical and computational mathematics is a broad topic; numerous algorithms exist for numerically solving the same mathematical problem. This courses focuses on algorithms for solving equations in one variable. Several algorithms exist for interpolating or extrapolating functions on the basis of a set of sample points of that function. Numerical methods for differentiation, but especially integration form a set of very important numerical algorithms. The course discusses numerous algorithms for solving ordinary differential equations.
profiles.judgment: Numerical integration, single-variable functions and differential equations. Supports modelling, not laboratory or physical theory.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops numerical methods for equations, differentiation and differential equations in scientific problems

profiles.name: Linear Systems
profiles.actualContent: The concepts of signals and systems appear in a wide variety of fields. The physical nature of the sig- nals to be acquired and the measurement systems may differ from application to application, but they all have in common that the signals contain information about the observed phenomenon and secondly, the systems respond to particular signals by producing other signals or certain behavior as output. This course discusses how to characterize alinear time-invariant systemand how it will respond to var- ious inputs. Theunit-impulse responseor - its equivalent in the frequency domain - thefrequency responsecharacterizes a linear time-invariant system. This course discussesconvolution. TheFourier series representationrepresents periodic signals as infinite harmonic series in continuous time and finite harmonic series in discrete time. Increasing the period of the periodic signals amounts to a denser Fourier series representation. In the limiting case that the period becomes infinitely long, the Fourier series rep- resentation becomes theFourier transform- both in continuous-time and in discrete-time. The course discusses the properties of the Fourier series representation and the Fourier transform in great detail. A very important characteristic of the Fourier transform is the duality property. TheLaplace transform generalizes the Fourier transform for continuous-time signals. In a very similar way, theZ-transform generalizes the Fourier transform for discrete-time signals.
profiles.judgment: Linear time-invariant systems, signals, convolution and Fourier/Laplace/Z transforms; no inferred nonlinear dynamics or quantum/advanced mechanics.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: studies signals, transfer functions, state-space models and differential equations for dynamic systems

profiles.name: Probability & Statistics
profiles.actualContent: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
profiles.judgment: Probability and mathematical statistics; useful general methods, not a physical-chemistry specialisation.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: provides probability, estimation and simulation for quantitative scientific research

profiles.name: The Science of Evolution
profiles.actualContent: The theory of evolution was contentious when it was first proposed by Darwin and Wallace in the 19th century. The human-centric view of the world would be replaced by the idea that random changes created everything in the world around us, including ourselves, something that did not quite sit right with society at large. Even today, there are many people in the world that do not believe that evolution explains our planet’s state of being. As the principles of evolution can be applied to any and all aspects, understanding how it has affected, and still affects, the world might very well be the most important part of any study in biology. In this course we will explore the topic of evolution from different angles and at different levels, from genes to populations, and cover the basics for all relevant aspects with regard to life on this planet. From the history through the mechanisms, we will familiarize ourselves with both the theoretical as well as the practical study of evolution, and gain an understanding of how we got here ourselves.
profiles.judgment: Evolutionary biology is genuine biological content, outside the defining physical-chemistry specialisation.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops evolutionary theory and the evidence used to explain biological change

profiles.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
profiles.actualContent: Ecology is the scientific study of the distribution and abundance of organisms and the interactions that determine distribution and abundance. Over the past decades, ecology has grown from an obscure science into a position at the forefront of public and political consciousness. Applied ecology has become an important scientific tool to address important political and environmental issues. Ecology is generally divided into 3 levels: the individual organism, the population (consisting of individuals of the same species) and the community, in which several species are living together. In addition, ecology focuses on the relationship between living creatures and their chemical and physical surroundings, which together make up an ecosystem. Ecology is a complex science. It draws on many areas of knowledge such as organic and inorganic chemistry, plant and animal biology, physiology, meteorology, and even economics. This course focuses on the basic principles of ecology, from individuals to ecosystems. We then proceed to environmental conditions and resources, and the 4 levels of ecology: individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems. Two weeks will be spent on ecological modelling, as an important tool for understanding and predicting ecological systems. We will conclude with some actual cases of applied ecology.
profiles.judgment: Population, community and ecosystem ecology and ecological modelling; not a substitute for chemical or physical theory.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: studies ecological processes from populations to ecosystems and introduces ecological modelling

profiles.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
profiles.actualContent: The production of food is a contentious topic in our modern society. Current farming methods are major contributors to environmental harm worldwide. However, the human population is expected to continue to grow to 10 billion before peaking, with the greatest growth forecast in developing countries. Sustainable farming is the approach where both food needs and environmental impact are balanced. As current farming practices are generally more concerned about output than impact, change is necessary to ensure a sustainable future, while still ensuring the human population can be fed adequately. In this course we will learn about and discuss different aspects of farming that contribute to future plans and directions of sustainable farming on a global scale. Current practices and environmental impacts will be presented, to understand where we are starting from. Current alternatives will be critically assessed, to understand how we might progress. Innovations and modern approaches will be researched, to understand where we might end up. The purpose of this course is not to convince you of what the right way forward is, but to present information objectively, so that you can make up your own mind and help build a more sustainable future.
profiles.judgment: Sustainable farming and agricultural innovation; meaningful applied environmental biology, not physical chemistry.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: applies biological and environmental science to sustainable agriculture and resource challenges

profiles.name: Dynamic Earth
profiles.actualContent: This course introduces you to the broad field of Earth Science. Earth Science in general and in all its sub disciplines is a very exciting and relevant field. You will never look at mountains, rivers and oceans in the same way after taking this course. You will discover in this course that many of the natural phenomena observed on (surface) and in (deep) the earth, are linked to processes of our Earth, that contrary to many other planets, is alive! The number of opportunities for employment in this field is increasing, because water, soil, mineral and fossil resources are limited. To limit the environmental impacts of our human endeavors new approaches are needed to counter water-soil-air pollution. Also, more efforts are needed to address the effects of the seemingly increased frequency of earthquakes, flooding, tsunamis and hurricanes. While studying the common geological phenomena, we will browse through major sub disciplines such as structural geology, mineralogy, petrology, earth history, geochemistry, geophysics, climatology, environmental geology, geohydrology, sedimentology, and resource management. Each one of these sub disciplines could easily fill a semester. At universities these sub-disciplines are usually taught by several professors that have specialized in one of the sub-disciplines. This course will be taught by professors partly based on the main division in Earth Science (surface earth disciplines) and Geophysics. Since geology is a typical outdoor science, you will not have a complete introduction without outdoor studies.
profiles.judgment: Earth science survey including geology, geophysics and geochemistry; survey breadth cannot stand in for sustained mechanics, electromagnetism or chemical analysis.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: introduces Earth materials and processes and the physical basis of natural phenomena without substituting for a physics course

profiles.name: Earth System Science Tools
profiles.actualContent: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.
profiles.judgment: Earth-system modelling, proxies and isotopic tools; genuine environmental methods with limited target overlap, not a general physical-chemistry laboratory sequence.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: uses modelling, proxies, isotope tracers and field evidence to investigate Earth-system processes

profiles.name: Environmental Biogeochemistry
profiles.actualContent: This course focusses on the biogeochemical processes on the earths surface. Most are related to soil-mineral-rock water interactions under near Earth -surface conditions. Biological and chemical controls on mineral formation processes will be studied in further detail as well as adsorption and leaching of nutrients or metals. Furthermore, (waste) -water treatment and engineered processes to recover valuable resources from waste, as well as some anthropogenic resource cycles are topics of this course. The theoretical and practical knowledge taught in SCIEART201/202 will be supplemented by using advanced geochemical modeling tools such as G eochemist Workbench. This course is very suitable for students in chemistry, geology and environmental science. The course may include some simple lab experiments, furthermore (in-class) exercises, one quiz and a case study.
profiles.judgment: Surface biogeochemistry, mineral-water interactions, geochemical modelling and possible simple experiments. Genuine chemistry contribution with environmental focus, not a synthesis/analytical/physical chemistry sequence.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: studies biological and chemical controls on Earth-surface processes and material cycles

profiles.name: Sustainability Essentials I
profiles.actualContent: ENSGATE101 - Sustainability Essentials serves as the Gateway course to all 200 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy all 200 level course in the cluster. We will use the model of planetary boundaries to discuss the concepts of sustainability with an anthropogenic focus. The planetary boundaries concept was presented in 2009 and provides a novel synthesis of the most pertinent global environmental challenges by analysing the risk of crossing critical thresholds in the behaviour of the Earth system’s processes. These boundaries act as a framework to define a "safe operating space for humanity," highlighting the limits within which human development can occur without causing catastrophic harm to the planet. 3
profiles.judgment: Planetary boundaries and sustainability foundations. Broad context, not the physics/chemistry/materials gateway content of the separate ENSGATE201 course.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: introduces Earth-system science, planetary boundaries and quantitative reasoning for environmental problems

profiles.name: Climate Change
profiles.actualContent: Climate change is the defining challenge of our time. It has large impacts on both the living and non-living Earth systems, as well as drives a number of profound societal transformations. This course is roughly divided in 3 parts. First, we will first focus on the drivers of anthropogenic climate change and its impacts on the natural world. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) the properties of greenhouse gases, sea level rise, ocean acidification, climate feedback loops and effects on various biome types. Secondly, we will discuss impacts on various aspects of society. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) food production, transportation, construction, health, and migration patterns. We will discuss climate governance and -justice. We will also look at the history of the climate change debate and identify strategies that have been deployed by interest groups to sow doubt and misinformation. Lastly, we will look into solutions for both adaptation and mitigation, such as renewable energy systems, carbon dioxide storage and climate-adaptive spatial planning. The course will include a number of guest lectures and excursions. After taking the course, you will be able to explain the fundamentals of climate change science. You will also be able to navigate a vast flow of information on climate change, and identify main and reliable sources; you will have insight in main climate change issues and have an overview of the pathways to mitigation and adaptation.
profiles.judgment: Climate science and sustainability provide relevant applications, not the required breadth and depth of physical chemistry.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: examines drivers and impacts of climate change across living and non-living Earth systems

profiles.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
profiles.actualContent: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor.
profiles.judgment: Team research on a Delta sustainability challenge with a regional partner; not the individual supervised physical-chemistry internship.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: conducts a team research project using research design, field evidence and data analysis on a sustainability problem

profiles.name: Functional Anatomy
profiles.actualContent: Functional Anatomy examines the structure of the human body in direct relation to function. In this course, anatomical structures and their functions are systematically studied together, at the level of body systems as well as individual anatomical components. The course is organised in thematic blocks, each addressing a specific anatomical region or system (the Skeletal System & Vertebral Column; Bony Thorax & Pelvis; Respiratory & Cardiovascular Systems; Abdomen; Reproductive & Lower Urinary Systems) and each emphasising specific anatomical and functional reasoning (rather than exhaustive memorisation). Within these blocks, learning activities are purposefully selected to support the intended learning outcomes, combining visual, spatial and experiential approaches. Anatomical understanding is developed through surface anatomy, medical imaging, scientific anatomical drawing and video-based human remain based material, complemented by carefully framed encounters with human skeletal remains, a dissection facility and in class clinical demonstrations. Together, these activities foster three-dimensional anatomical insight, spatial reasoning and awareness of anatomical variation. Please note that these are explicitly framed as academic learning experiences rather than clinical skills training. Studying human anatomy inevitably confronts students with an ethical paradox: respect for the human body is taught through its objectification for scientific study.
profiles.judgment: Functional human anatomy, imaging and demonstrations; no inferred comparative physiology, chemistry or physical theory.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: connects human structure to function through anatomy, dissection material and imaging

profiles.name: Pharmacology
profiles.actualContent: Pharmacology is the science of drugs including their origin, composition, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity (Merriam-Webster Learner’s Dictionary). The functioning of the (diseased) human body can be affected by (medicinal) drugs, which act through a variety of molecular mechanisms. In this course, the basic principles of pharmacology will be discussed, followed by studies of different aspects of drugs and the human body to illustrate the se pharmacological principles which are used for rational drug develo pment and physiological use. The importance of neuronal, hormonal, immunological (whole body) and biochemical (whole cell) regulation for proper physiological and cellular function, and dysregulation during pathological processes are emphasized. Identification of potential drug t argets and the interaction of drugs with macromolecules (enzymes, cell surface receptors, and signaling molecules) as the main pharmacological principles are central in this course. Quantitative pharmacological, pharmacokinetic and statistical methods are used. At the end of the course you will be able to explain effectiv ely existing drug therapies in a rational way in terms of molecular targets, cellular actions and physiological consequences of pharmacological treatment. They will be able to suggest targets for drug development on the basis of pathophysiological insights a nd to apply pharmacological models when describing concentration-response, time-concentration, and time-response relationships of drugs.
profiles.judgment: Pharmacology and pharmacokinetic models. Genuine biomedical substance, not chemical synthesis, medicinal chemistry or physical organic chemistry.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: studies drug targets, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic action and toxicity

profiles.name: Infection & Immunity
profiles.actualContent: Infectious diseases and disorders of the immune system are a continuous threat to the life and well-being of humans, animals and plants. Studying the fundamental processes in immunology, such as the recognition of self and non-self (e.g. microbes), development of mature lymphocyte receptor repertoires, and the innate and adaptive immune response is crucial for the understanding how the immune system deals with the daily threat of microorganisms. On the other hand, general knowledge of the highly diverse mic robial world is needed. From this knowledge, detailed specific understanding of microbial strategies to circumvent host resistance can be acquired. As a principle, the course will focus on interactions between host and infectious agents. Basic principles a s microbial virulence, inflammatory responses, tissue damage and apoptosis are discussed. In addition to normal immune responses to infectious agents, the course will also deal with immunopathological processes and diseases.
profiles.judgment: Infection and immunity; genuine biomedical specialisation, not physical-chemistry depth.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: examines host–pathogen interactions and molecular and cellular immune responses

profiles.name: Mechanisms of Disease
profiles.actualContent: In this course the relation between the normal function (physiology) and disease (pathophysiology) is illustrated for six basal organ systems: 1. cardiovascular, 2. lung (pulmonology), 3. kidney (nephrology), 4. digestive tract, 5. endocrine glands (endocrinology) and 6. central nervous system. The aim of this course is to provide insight in the principles of the mechanisms of diseases. For the organ systems mentioned the student first has to study the embryology and anatomy, Using this information as starting point, the basic physiology is studied and using the combined knowledge the student must be able to derive the symptoms and failures in the system or the pathophysiology.
profiles.judgment: Organ-system pathophysiology; genuine biomedical content with little direct physical-chemistry contribution.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: relates normal physiology to cellular and organ-system disease mechanisms

profiles.name: Neurobiology
profiles.actualContent: Cognitive neuroscience uses inputs and perspectives from many disciplines, such as psychology, biology, medicine, computer science, and philosophy. In this course, the focus will be on the biology side of neuroscience. As a result, we will focus on evoluti onary pressures on animals in general, resulting in specific behaviors and physiological processes in these animals and ourselves. In this light, you will gain a greater understanding of biorhythms and natural behaviors, and eventually of specific disorders and diseases. Additionally, we will take a look at the use of animals in neuroscientific research, such as rodents, and discuss ethical and welfare implications. We will also familiarize you with experimental techniques in the laboratory, such as cell st aining and using a microscope, and compare the (brain) anatomy of different animal species. This course will familiarize you with concepts and skills required within the discipline of Neurobiology. A selected number of key topics within the field will be discussed, including comparative anatomy, biorhythms, animal models and ethics, and disorders . The course also includes guest lectures and practical work such as labwork, group assignments and student presentations.
profiles.judgment: Neurobiology and practical staining/microscopy; genuine biological exposure, not physics of neurons or electromagnetic theory.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: examines neural cells, comparative neuroanatomy, microscopy and experimental neurobiology

profiles.name: Perception & Action
profiles.actualContent: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
profiles.judgment: Sensory and motor neuroscience; genuine neural systems content, not neurophysics.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: studies neural mechanisms of sensory processing, perception and action

profiles.name: Higher Order Functions
profiles.actualContent: This course builds upon the knowledge gained in the introductory course in Cognitive Science. It will deepen your knowledge of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Also, your knowledge of experimental approaches in the field of cognitive neuroscience will be enhanced; such that you become able to evaluate research findings and to design your own experiments. A selected number of higher order cognitive processes will be dealt with, including memory, emotion, social cognition, attention, consciousness, decision making and planning. In addition to established knowledge, current research questions will be discussed in depth.
profiles.judgment: Higher cognitive function and experimental design; distinct from physical mechanisms, chemical analysis and synthesis.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: deepens neurophysiology, neuroanatomy and experimental study of higher cognition

profiles.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
profiles.actualContent: Have you ever wondered what makes life on earth possible? The foundation of life, health & biomedical science course takes you on a journey into the building blocks of life, exploring how cells, molecules, and systems interact to create and sustain living organisms. Cells are at the heart of this story: they are the basic units of life, taking in energy and nutrients from their environment and converting them into biologically useful forms. Inside every cell lies genetic information, dna, that not only directs all cellular activities but also passes traits from one generation to the next. Mutations, recombination and epigenetics create variation, and this diversity fuels the evolutionary process through natural selection. The course is structured in four interconnected units: The cell as a unit of life Basic molecular biology Cellular physiology and communication Capita selecta (a series of explorations that give you a first taste of the diverse academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.) You will also work on a special research presentation assignment, which allows you to engage with scientific literature, reflect on how we know what we know, and experience how new knowledge can be generated. But this course is more than just an introduction. As a gateway course, foundation of life, health & biomedical science opens the door to exciting academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.
profiles.judgment: Cellular and molecular life-science foundations support the biological interface; no chemical-analysis/synthesis/physics lab claim.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: introduces cells, molecules, genetics, physiology, microorganisms and experimental biomedical reasoning

profiles.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
profiles.actualContent: This 100-level course ‘Introduction to Brain & Behavior’ constitutes the Gateway Course for the Cluster Health, Cognition and Behavior: Units ‘Cognitive Science’ and ‘Clinical Psychology’. In this course you will gain foundational knowledge and essential skills that you will need in intermediate and advanced courses of these units. We will look at the various ways in which psychologists and neuroscientists have approached questions such as: Why do people behave the way they do? Can we predict behavior and mental processes in a particular situation, for example after brain damage? Is it possible to change these behaviors and mental processes? How do nature and nurture interact in the development of how we think, feel and behave? Which areas of the brain serve which function, and how do neurons communicate with each other and with the body? We will explore these complex and fascinating topics together from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective, learning about functional brain anatomy on a micro and macro scale, research methodologies and tools in the fields of Cognitive Science and Clinical Psychology, as well as main psychological theories and the relevance of main clinical skills in Psychology. The course will be organized including a combination of different methods of teaching and learning; e.g. interactive lectures, individual and team activities with a collaborative learning methodology, guest lectures, reflective activities, among others. Course outline HCBGATE102 Introduction to Brain & Behavior Page 2 of 16
profiles.judgment: Brain, cognition and behaviour foundation; coherent neuroscience preparation, not natural-science physical theory.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: provides a biological and psychological foundation for the neurobiology direction

profiles.name: Molecular Cell Biology
profiles.actualContent: New discoveries and advancements in scientific research are proposed every day, all around us. It can be overwhelming to keep up. This course provides the foundation for students to understand a vast array of practical applications in a multitude of life science topics (e.g. industry, medicine, agriculture, ecology, etc.). Students w ill take a closer look at the cellular biology of mostly eukaryotes, but also prokaryotes, gaining a comprehensive understanding of cell structure and physio logy. Concepts from the LIFE101 course, Introduction to Life Sciences, will be revisited and students will dive deeper into the details of life processes to understand the underlying molecular mechanisms. Students will also learn to examine current research topics and methods used to study the invisible world of molecular biology. Students will be encouraged to question the reproducibility of results and to propose how modernization of existing methods (and/or theoretical) technologies would improve the limitations of research and the validity of results. The course consists of five themes: 1 – The fundamental units of life: Cellular components, chemistry and energetics 2 – Genomes: DNA to Proteins, replication, repair and regulation of gene expression 3 – Cellular dynamics: Membrane trafficking, transport and signaling pathways 4 – Cell fate: Cell division, tissues, stem cells and cancer 5 – Drug Mechanisms (Paper and Poster Project)
profiles.judgment: Molecular cell biology, gene regulation, membranes and current research; genuine molecular contribution, not chemical bonding or organic synthesis.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops cell structure, gene expression, signalling, division and molecular-cell methods

profiles.name: Human Physiology
profiles.actualContent: Physiology is the study of the normal functioning of a living organism and its component parts, including all its chemical and physical processes. In this course, the focus is on the function of the adult human body and of different organ systems. Knowledge of the subject is essential for students with a medical interest and recommended for every student interested in the function (s) of the (own) human body. The course includes fundamental concepts of molecules, cellular and systems physiology to understand how the human body functions and maintains a steady state. Although some medical examples are used to illustrate general physiological principles, this is not a course in medical physiology. Still, the core of physiological knowledge you will learn by ta king Human Physiology will help you better understand human health and disease. The course will be divided in 4 units: (1) Basic cell processes , (2) Homeostasis and control, (3) Integration of function , and (4) Metabolism, growth, and aging . In addition there will be one individual assignment. Contents of the 4 course units are structure-function relationships (organelles, cells, tissues, organs), energy handling, homeostasis and control systems, signaling and communication, study of individual organ systems (cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine, muscles, nervous, digestive, reproduction), and integration of functions.
profiles.judgment: Human physiology: genuine biological systems teaching; not general comparative physiology or physical theory.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: examines the chemical and physical processes underlying integrated human physiology

profiles.name: Biochemistry
profiles.actualContent: Living organisms evolved from the prebiotic world through chemical reactions. Laws governing those early reactions are the same t oday. C hemistry is the underlying science behind biology. Biochemistry, the chemistry of life, deals with the reactions that produce the molecules of life: proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids that enable the self -assembly and reproduction of simple and complex organisms. Although organisms vary en ormously in complexity and biological properties, all domains of life use similar biomolecules for encoding and transmitting information, intra - and intercellular signaling, formation of membranes, building and degrading macromolecules, energy metabolism, and many more features. Errors in the production, proper localization or degradation of these molecules can often lead to disease. Biochemical knowledge is not only essential for understanding and treating these diseases, but also necessary for advancing many applications in biotechnology.
profiles.judgment: Biomolecules, reactions, metabolism and molecular mechanisms: a strong genuine biochemistry contribution. One course cannot sustain the separate analytical, organic and physical chemistry sequences.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: covers biomolecules, metabolic pathways, nucleic acids and biochemical mechanisms

profiles.name: Life Science Laboratory
profiles.actualContent: This course is designed for a broad group of UCR students interested in life sciences. This course provides an introduction to the biochemical and molecular laboratory work performed in most labs today, and hence is a highly recommended course for all life science and medical track students. The students will be introduced to the following themes: • Blood • Bacteria, handling hygiene and genetically modified organisms (GMOs) • Protein production, isolation and analysis • DNA isolation and analysis (digestion, PCR and gel electrophoresis) • Bioinformatics These themes are characteristic or representative of basic biological and clinical research. Additional clinical diagnostic themes are added whenever there is an opportunity. The concepts, principles and techniques used in this course regarding blood and blood proteins include a basic blood cell analysis (hemogram), protein electrophoresis, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and a patient case. Course outline HCBLIFE214; Life Science Laboratory Page 2 of 8 With respect to bacteria, students will first learn the skills for properly handling pure cultures. A series of tests will also be carried out to check hygiene and sterilization procedures, bacterial species determination and the effect of antibiotics on bacterial growth. It also includes genetic modification of bacteria using safe microbiological techniques. After students have become acquainted with the safe handling of bacteria, they will generate a genetically modified organism (GMO).
profiles.judgment: Blood/bacterial/protein/DNA techniques, PCR, electrophoresis and bioinformatics: genuine molecular laboratory skills, distinct from chemical analysis, synthesis and physics laboratories.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: provides biochemical and molecular laboratory work, bioinformatics and experimental interpretation

profiles.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
profiles.actualContent: This course covers a vast number of topics from general and molecular pathology and genetics of humans. The pathology portion includes the bases of pathology which is cell injury and cell death. The pathology also covers how acute and chronic inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration and fibrosis, and neoplasia contribute to pathologies. The course then shifts to understanding the molecular genetics underlying disease. The significance of chromosome structure and organization of genes will be covered along with gene mutations (and their inheritance) through several examples of genetic diseases. The course also focuses on the status of genetic testing and genetic treatments. Ethical and legal considerations for now and in the future will also be examined.
profiles.judgment: Molecular pathology, disease mechanisms and genetics; substantive molecular biology without physical-chemistry specialisation.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: examines human genetics, cellular injury, inflammation, tissue repair and molecular pathology

profiles.name: Advanced Research Seminar
profiles.actualContent: This course will introduce you to methods to perform systematic reviews and meta-analysis: the statistical analyses that are used to synthesize summary data from multiple of studies. Meta-analysis and systematic reviews are being used in many disciplines, including psychology, medicine, education, and others. Meta-Analysis and systematic reviews are very important tools in evidence based policy making as they allow to combine results of existing studies fairly objectively, to establish general treatment effect (effect size) and degree to which effect size is robust and consistent across the kinds of studies sampled. Participants will get hands-on experience in performing analyses using R. R is leading language in statistical computing. R is an open source language with huge number of individual and institutional users. The introduction to will help you the understand basics of R: program interface, syntax, variables and operations, reading data into R, accessing R packages, how to handle data structures, and create own functions. You will get acquainted with community developed packages providing common statistical analyses and practice conducting meta-analysis using R. The course is active learning oriented, with you presenting and performing preforming tasks in the class. As it is a 300 level course you are expected to take the responsibility for your learning and proactive attitude: come prepared to the class, complete homework/practice exercise and actively search answers to your questions and unclarified issues.
profiles.judgment: Systematic review and meta-analysis using R; research synthesis is not an individual theoretical or practical physical-chemistry project.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops systematic-review and meta-analytic methods for synthesising biomedical and behavioural evidence

boundedCatalogueScan.actualContent: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.

boundedCatalogueScan.actualContent: In this course you will learn how to function in a 'real-world' design and development environment. Hence, you will work in a group that mimics a design and development (d&d) team as e.g. in industry. The members of a team in this course fulfill roles similarly as occur in industrial d&d teams (e.g. chair person, secretary, ...). A team is responsible for much of its own planning. The functioning of a team involves e.g. preparing agendas for team meetings, taking minutes, planning practical work, maintaining a documentation system, etc. During the course, the instructor will NOT act as chairperson / team leader, but rather as an ‘external consultant'. During the course we will go through the various phases of the development of a consumer product: assessment of customer needs and translating these into a product concept, develop a method to make a product, both on laboratory- as on industrial scale, analyzing environmental impact, analyzing costs and proceeds. In a d&d project and hence in the course, activities are quite varied, and include interviewing potential customers, laboratory experiments, constructing quantitative mathematical model(s) of the working mechanism(s) of a product, constructing a prototype, work out how a product can be produced on an industrial scale, consider protection of intellectual property etc.. In this course, in addition to the more traditional aspects of the d&d process, special attention will be given to sustainability. This involves e.g. the nature of the materials used (natural, recycled, …), lifespan, repairability, 'circularity' etc.
boundedCatalogueScan.judgment: Consumer product design team, laboratory/model/prototype work and sustainability. Genuine design practice, not physics/chemistry disciplinary depth.

boundedCatalogueScan.actualContent: To prepare our society for a circular and sustainable future, we need to evaluate the environmental impact of products, processes, or services throughout their entire lifecycle, from raw material extraction to final disposal, or ideally re-usage as new raw materials. To do this, we have to understand the environmental, social and health consequences of products and processes and develop a strategic planning for future activi- ties. ENSSUST112 - Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economywill be heavily focussed on “learning by doing”, rather than by just studying books. Therefore most of this course will consist of analysing different products, processes and services and include guest lectures by experts working in the field of sustainability and circularity. 3
boundedCatalogueScan.judgment: Life-cycle impacts/circular planning and hands-on analyses, not chemical or physical experimental instruction.
